title: Spatiotemporal Imaging of Thermally Driven Metal-Insulator Phase Domain Propagation in VO2
authors: Ilaria Delbono, Raouf Amara, Matias Feldman, Hankun Yang, Cédric Leau, Carlo Scian, Erwan Dandeu, Sébastien Royer, Debora Pierucci, Emmanuel Lhuillier, Franck Vidal, Tiziana Cesca, Hilton B. de Aguiar, Jose Ordonez-Miranda, Danièle Fournier, Raj Pandya, Boris Kalinic, Giovanni Mattei, James K. Utterback
abstract: Achieving a detailed picture of the nature and dynamics of phase boundaries remains a major challenge, particularly solid-solid transitions central to phase-change materials. Here, we use stroboscopic optical scattering microscopy and finite-element simulations to study the nonlinear thermally driven motion of the mesoscale insulator-metal phase boundary in VO2 thin films. We visualize the lateral spatiotemporal evolution of a diffraction-limited photoinduced metallic phase domain, resolving its outward propagation, contraction, and ultimate disappearance. The phase boundary dynamics are governed by heat flow, which can be controlled by excitation fluence, film thickness, and substrate thermal conductivity. Parameter-free agreement between the data and nonlinear thermal transport simulations identify the phase boundary transport as locally diffusive under this regime. We quantify how the latent heat acts as a thermal inertia, suppressing transport and prolonging the phase coexistence. Paradoxically, despite being driven by the underlying thermal gradient locally described by Fourier's law, the mesoscale phase front propagates faster than expected from thermal diffusion. This phenomenon arises from the distinction between temperature-field evolution and phase-boundary isotherm motion. These results establish a link between heat dissipation and mesoscale phase-front motion, providing a framework for controlling phase-transition kinetics relevant to photonics applications of VO2. We anticipate that this approach generalizes to a broad class of first- and second-order transitions.
summary: This work uses advanced optical microscopy and thermal simulations to map the dynamics of the metal-insulator phase boundary in VO2. It demonstrates that the phase front motion is fundamentally controlled by heat dissipation, establishing a quantitative link between thermal transport and phase-transition kinetics. This framework is valuable for controlling phase-change materials for photonic applications.
main_problem: The study investigates the nature and dynamics of the mesoscale, thermally driven propagation of the insulator-metal phase boundary in VO2 thin films.
main_result: The phase front propagation is governed by heat flow, and while it can propagate faster than predicted by simple thermal diffusion, the dynamics are successfully modeled by linking heat dissipation to the phase-front motion.
method: The research combines stroboscopic optical scattering microscopy for in-situ spatiotemporal imaging with finite-element simulations of nonlinear, latent-heat-modulated thermal transport.
model_or_system: The system is VO2 thin films undergoing a first-order solid-solid phase transition. The modeling incorporates nonlinear thermal transport, latent heat effects, and the distinction between temperature-field evolution and phase-boundary isotherm motion.
key_observables: Lateral spatiotemporal evolution of the metallic phase domain, phase boundary position, instantaneous effective diffusivity ($D_{	ext{eff}}(t)$), and reflectance change ($\Delta R/R_0$).
important_parameters: Excitation fluence, film thickness, substrate thermal conductivity, and the latent heat of the transition.
main_assumptions: The approach assumes the dynamics can be described by heat flow governed by Fourier's law, and that the phase boundary motion can be characterized by an effective diffusivity.
figures_summary: Figures show the spatiotemporal dynamics of the metal-insulator boundary using stroboSCAT, and supplementary figures compare experimental and simulated instantaneous diffusivity ($D_{	ext{eff}}(t)$) derived from the evolution of the domain radius.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the experimental setup and observes the domain evolution. It then develops theoretical models comparing instantaneous diffusivity versus velocity, showing that diffusivity is the key parameter. Finally, it applies these models to analyze the experimental data, confirming the link between heat dissipation and phase-front kinetics.
why_interesting: The work provides a detailed, quantitative framework for understanding non-equilibrium phase transitions driven by thermal gradients, which has parallels in studying quench dynamics or domain wall motion in other condensed matter systems.
